title: Vertical Order and Tree Views
summary: The "view" family of problems: reading a tree from a direction instead of an order — left/right/top/bottom view, vertical order, boundary, and diagonal traversal.

slides.markdown:
Every traversal so far in this group answers "in what **order** should I visit nodes." This topic asks a different question: "what does the tree look like from a given **direction** — the side, the top, the bottom?" That reframing turns out to have a clean answer for most of these problems: assign each node a **coordinate** (usually a column index, sometimes a row too), then group or pick nodes by that coordinate instead of by traversal order.

Once coordinates are assigned, view problems become bookkeeping problems — which node wins a given column, which tie-breaking rule applies — rather than needing a new traversal algorithm each time.

slides.subTitle: Via BFS (last/first per level) or DFS (depth-first-seen)
slides.markdown:
The **right view** is the last node visible at each level when looking from the right — equivalently, the last node processed at each level in a standard level-order BFS. The **left view** is the mirror: the first node at each level.

A DFS alternative works too, and it's worth knowing because it generalizes better to some variants: traverse right-child-first, then left-child-first, tracking the maximum depth seen so far — the first node encountered at each new depth is that level's right-view (or left-view, if traversing left-first) answer, since DFS with the right ordering visits each level's "view node" before any other node at that depth.

slides.sectionTitle: Right side view using level-order traversal

slides.subTitle: Enabling top/bottom/vertical problems
slides.markdown:
The root gets column 0. Every left move decreases the column by 1; every right move increases it by 1 — row is just depth, incrementing by 1 on every move regardless of direction. This single coordinate assignment, computed with one traversal (BFS or DFS, either works), is the foundation every problem in this topic builds on.

Once every node has a (row, column) pair, "vertical order" is just "group nodes by column, and within a column, order by row (and some tie-break for equal row-and-column)." "Top view" is "per column, keep only the smallest-row node." "Bottom view" is the mirror — largest row per column. The hard traversal problem has been converted into a straightforward grouping problem.

slides.subTitle: Column-grouped BFS with stable tie-breaking

slides.sectionTitle: Top view ties at the same column
slides.subTitle: Why BFS order (not DFS) decides the correct answer
slides.markdown:
For top view, when two nodes land in the same column at the same row (a genuine tie, common when a node's right child and its sibling's left child share a column), the tie-break rule is: whichever was discovered **first** wins. Using DFS discovery order for this is a common bug — DFS can visit a deeper-column-matching node from an entirely different branch before it visits the shallower, earlier node that should actually win, because DFS commits to one path before exploring siblings.

BFS discovery order resolves this correctly for free: since BFS processes strictly level by level, and left-to-right within a level, the first node recorded for a given column at the topmost row is guaranteed to be the one that should be visible from above — no extra tie-breaking logic needed beyond "first write wins" using a BFS-ordered scan.

slides.subTitle: Same coordinates, opposite tie-breaking rule
slides.markdown:
| | Top view | Bottom view |
|---|---|---|
| Per-column winner | smallest row (topmost) | largest row (bottommost) |
| Tie-break when rows are equal | first discovered (BFS order) wins | last discovered (BFS order) wins |
| Implementation change from the other | none beyond swapping the winner rule | none beyond swapping the winner rule |

Both views use the identical coordinate assignment and the identical BFS discovery pass — the *only* difference is which node a column keeps when there's competition: top view keeps the shallowest, bottom view keeps the deepest (and for bottom view specifically, "last write wins" during a BFS scan naturally implements "keep the deepest" without extra row-comparison logic, since deeper rows are discovered later).

slides.subTitle: Left edge + leaves + right edge, without double-counting corners
slides.markdown:
Boundary traversal outputs the root, the entire left edge (top to bottom, excluding leaves), all leaves left to right, then the entire right edge (bottom to top, excluding leaves) — traced as a single continuous loop around the tree's outline.

The detail that causes bugs: a node can qualify as **both** a boundary node and a leaf (the leftmost or rightmost leaf, for instance), and including it twice — once in the edge pass, once in the leaf pass — double-counts it. The standard fix explicitly excludes leaves from the left/right edge collection, treating the leaf pass as the sole authority on which leaves appear, and lets the edge passes only ever contribute non-leaf boundary nodes.

slides.subTitle: Grouping nodes that share a diagonal slope
slides.markdown:
Diagonal traversal groups nodes by a different coordinate than vertical order: instead of column (which changes on both left and right moves), it tracks a value that only changes on **left** moves — a right move keeps the same diagonal, a left move starts a new one.

Concretely: assign the root diagonal 0; a right child inherits its parent's diagonal unchanged, a left child gets `parent's diagonal + 1`. Nodes sharing a diagonal value form one output group, in discovery order. This is the same coordinate-assignment idea as vertical order, just with a different rule for how the coordinate changes per move — reinforcing that most of these "view" problems are variations on one technique (assign a coordinate, group by it) rather than unrelated algorithms.

slides.sectionTitle: Using DFS recursion depth as a stand-in for BFS level
slides.subTitle: Where view answers silently break
slides.markdown:
A subtle bug across several view problems: using DFS recursion depth to track "how far down" a node is, while relying on **DFS visitation order** to break ties — the two don't compose correctly, because DFS depth is accurate but DFS visitation order isn't the same left-to-right, shallowest-first guarantee BFS provides.

Concretely, for top view: if you traverse DFS left-then-right and use "first write wins" per column, a node from a *deeper* level down the left branch can get recorded before a *shallower* node down the right branch simply because DFS reaches it first in traversal order — producing a wrong "topmost" answer, since DFS's visitation order has no relationship to row/depth ordering across different branches. The fix is either genuinely using BFS for view problems that need shallowest-wins tie-breaking, or, if DFS is preferred, explicitly comparing recorded depths rather than relying on visitation order alone to imply depth order.
